correctness.rationale: Every one of 4096 labelled binary states on the explicitly defined 12-vertex 5-regular icosahedral graph is enumerated. A separate symbolic ring-inequality argument proves the unique-predecessor property of every nonunanimous cap. The finite transition table checks F^7=F^5, 14 fixed states equal to the 12 closed neighborhoods plus unanimity, 156 normalized primitive two-cycles, exact first-entry and basin histograms, and isolated cap basins. A separate 30-edge construction and vertex-by-vertex majority routine reproduces the result, confirms isomorphism with the canonical icosahedral graph, verifies all 120 automorphisms and seven temporal-cycle geometric orbits. The included 82 geometric state-orbit rows total 4096 states; all proof code and outputs are present. Finite exhaustive verification proves this exact finite claim, not an infinite theorem.

originality.rationale: Directed semantic searches of mathematical records, web literature, and OEIS found no equivalent icosahedral binary-majority transition/basin census. The strongest relevant general qualitative theorem (Goles–Olivos) implies period at most two, not the present enumerations or sharp entrance. Benjamini et al. addresses unimodular and random graphs. Dodecahedral majority and icosahedral Greenberg–Hastings counts are on different graphs or for a different update rule and do not imply these numbers. The complete Goles–Olivos original article was not inspected, so historical priority remains qualified. The full relevant 1988 Agur–Fraenkel–Klein fixed-point article was inspected; its one-dimensional self-inclusive three-bit update is inapplicable to the icosahedron.
residual_risks: The complete original Goles–Olivos (1980) article was unavailable; historical priority cannot be declared certain.
Unindexed or inaccessible publications might contain an equivalent small-graph census.
The mathematical proof is reproducible and exhaustive but not independently audited by another party.

value.rationale: The ordinary icosahedron is a canonical, maximally symmetric, planar 5-regular Platonic graph: a natural exact benchmark for majority vote. The result is a complete discrete dynamical atlas of all 4096 states, not a selected easy statistic. It discovers 12 locally stable balanced states with no transient ancestors, alongside two huge consensus basins, a rich four-size oscillatory basin spectrum, seven inequivalent geometries, and a sharp finite entrance-time profile. These effects are not implied by generic convergence and are of use in studying geometric constraints on consensus and validating finite-network dynamics methods. The result makes no unsupported infinite-family claim.
